intro: Jalhay sits on the edge of the Hautes Fagnes, and its best-known tree is the largest multi-trunk oak in Belgium. Les Sept Frères de Gospinal was cut back in the eighteenth century and regrew as seven fused trunks, 7.67 metres round; one is now dead. A short walk through the same forest finds Clawé Fawe, a beech villagers once drove nails into to cure a toothache, at the same old communal border. Both stand on trails near the Hautes Fagnes, free to reach on foot.
meta_description: Les Sept Frères de Gospinal, Belgium's largest multi-trunk oak, and Clawé Fawe, a beech nail tree, on forest trails near the Hautes Fagnes.
question_meta: Les Sept Frères de Gospinal, over 300 years old, is Belgium's largest multi-trunk oak: seven fused trunks 7.67 metres round near Jalhay.
question_answer: Jalhay's oldest confirmed tree is Les Sept Frères de Gospinal, a pedunculate oak on the trail between Jalhay and Solwaster, opposite the Gospinal forestry house. Its fused trunks measured 7.67 metres round in 2021, making it the largest multi-trunk oak recorded in Belgium. It is over 300 years old.
question_context:
The name, the seven brothers, describes what happened after the tree was cut back in the mid-eighteenth century: rather than dying, it regrew as seven trunks, since fused into one body large enough that a nineteenth-century lawyer is said to have received clients inside it. It also served as the meeting point where Sart and Jalhay argued out their shared boundary. A 2012 ministerial order recorded 7.44 metres round; a 2021 visit measured 7.67, roughly a centimetre a year of growth in between. The site sign is blunt: over 300 years old, nearing the end of its life, one of the seven trunks already dead, though the canopy is still vibrant. It stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the trail between Jalhay and Solwaster.

A short walk through the same patch of forest finds Clawé Fawe, a beech at a crossroads north of the hamlet of Foyr. Villagers once drove nails into it to draw out a toothache, and it also marked the boundary between Jalhay and neighbouring Limbourg, at the site of Jalhay's old gibbet. It is 3.79 metres round and nobody has recorded its age.

faq.q: How old is Les Sept Frères de Gospinal?
faq.a: Over 300 years, according to the sign at the site. It was cut back in the mid-eighteenth century and regrew as seven trunks that have since fused into one.

faq.q: Why is it called the seven brothers?
faq.a: The original trunk was cut back around the mid-1700s and regrew as seven separate stems, which have since fused into a single body 7.67 metres round, the largest multi-trunk oak recorded in Belgium.
Yes, though it is declining. One of the seven trunks is dead and the site sign says it is nearing the end of its life, but a 2021 visit still found the rest of the canopy vibrant.

The tree stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the marked walking trail between Jalhay and Solwaster, near the Hautes Fagnes. There is no public transport stop at the site; it is reached on foot.

faq.q: Is there another old tree near Les Sept Frères de Gospinal?
faq.a: Yes. Clawé Fawe, a beech nail tree, stands at a forest crossroads a short walk away, north of the hamlet of Foyr. It has its own story: villagers drove nails into it to cure a toothache.

trees.name: Les Sept Frères de Gospinal

location.address: Opposite the Gospinal forestry house, between Jalhay and Solwaster, near the Hautes Fagnes

trees.story:
A nineteenth-century lawyer who owned the Gospinal estate received his clients inside this oak. There was room. Cut back in the middle of the eighteenth century, it regrew as seven trunks that have since fused into one body 7.67 metres round, the largest multi-trunk oak in Belgium, and the reason it is called Les Sept Frères, the seven brothers.

It did other public work too. Officials of the communes of Sart and Jalhay used it as their meeting point when they argued out where the boundary between them ran.

The measurements are recent and they agree with each other. The ministerial order that made it a protected monument in 2012 records a girth of 7.44 metres; a visit in 2021 measured 7.67 at seventy centimetres from the ground, roughly a centimetre a year of new wood in between. It stands 26 metres tall. Wallonia had already classified it as a remarkable tree back in 1987.

The sign on site is blunt about the rest: over 300 years old, and nearing the end of its life. One of the seven trunks is dead and the others carry old wounds, though the account of that 2021 visit describes the canopy as still vibrant. Both of those things are true at once.

It stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the walking trail between Jalhay and Solwaster near the Hautes Fagnes.
trees.access: Free, beside a public nature-walking trail near the Hautes Fagnes.
trees.transport: On a marked walking trail between Jalhay and Solwaster; no public transport stop at the site, reached on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the seven trunks fused into a single body 7.67 metres round near the base, one of them dead. It stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the trail between Jalhay and Solwaster.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: Clawé Fawe (the nail tree of Foyr)

location.address: Forest crossroads in the Bois de Foyr, north of the hamlet of Foyr, Jalhay

trees.story:
People drove nails into this beech to get rid of their toothache. The idea, common across the Ardennes, was that the ailment passed out of the body and into the wood, and the name Clawé Fawe, the nailed beech, records what the tree was for.

It had other jobs, most of them grimmer. It marked the boundary between Jalhay, which answered to the Prince-Bishop of Liège, and Limbourg, which answered to the Duchy of Brabant, two communes with a long history of not getting along. And it stood at the site of Jalhay's gibbet. The present tree replaced an older one that did the same work, until the French cut it down at the end of the eighteenth century.

Belgium has around 59 known nail trees, 33 of them in the province of Liège, and this is one of the named ones. It is a European beech, 3.79 metres round at chest height when it was measured in July 2013.

It stands at a forest crossroads north of the hamlet of Foyr, on marked walking trails between Jalhay and the Hautes Fagnes, a short way through the same woods from Les Sept Frères. The two sources that place it disagree by about a hundred metres, so the pin gets you to the right patch of forest and the crossroads does the rest.

Nobody has published an age for this beech. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.access: Free, at a forest crossroads reached by marked walking trails near Jalhay and the Hautes Fagnes; open at all times, no ticket.
trees.transport: On a forest path north of the hamlet of Foyr, between Jalhay and the Hautes Fagnes; no public transport stop at the site, reached on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the beech at the forest crossroads, 3.79 metres round at chest height, unlike the multi-trunked oak of Les Sept Frères nearby. It stands north of the hamlet of Foyr.
